The House of Habsburg. One of Europe's most powerful and longest-reigning dynasties, the Habsburgs rose from obscurity in a small Swiss canton to become rulers of Austria by the fourteenth century. They expanded their territories not through conquest, but through shrewd marriage alliances that accumulated lands across three continents.

From 1438 onwards, the Habsburgs produced the Holy Roman Emperors continuously until the empire's dissolution in 1806. They also ruled the Spanish Empire from 1516 to 1700 under Charles V and his successors, controlling Spain, the Netherlands, parts of Italy, and Spanish America. Maria Theresa, born in 1717 and reigning until 1780, modernized the Austrian state, reformed its military, and fought the War of Austrian Succession to retain Habsburg territories against Prussia.

In 1867, the Austro-Hungarian Empire was formed as their final and second-largest realm, stretching across Central and Eastern Europe with the dual monarchy of Austria and Hungary. As Catholics, the Habsburgs played a central role in the Counter-Reformation and the Thirty Years' War. But the dynasty's end came swiftly. When Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in 1914, it triggered World War I and ultimately led to the collapse of the dynasty in 1918.
